title: Reflecting on my research intrests
body:
My research trajectory has never remained stagnant, it’s “cool” way to start,  I know. Some might even call it a mercurial pursuit, hinting at a lack of long-term commitment. However, I firmly believe that this fluidity is a strength, that will allow me to survive and thrive across domains but with knowledge and right skills indeed. My words definitely made you realize that I am a early stage researcher from GenZ.
 
I am constantly moved and motivated by the sheer volume of “cool” developments happening over the years. I agree with the traditional view that a tree with deep, established roots is harder to remove than one with shallow, surface level roots. Yet we know both can flourish depending on the environment and luck. I didn't believe in luck for long time but I have realized how crazy luck can work, I hope we all get lucky - coz why not!!!!
Being a jack in all trades in research doesn't mean master of none, I believe that I am agile enough to adapt.I'm not attempting to justify this path, instead I am embracing the journey of discovering my true interests. While my research journey seem chaotic, I truly feel I am in the right and the wrong era at the same time. 

Finally coming to main objective of writing this blog. My research interests lie in the following areas and I created this page to sum up my perspective and summary of the literature I have,am and will be exploring.

title: Semiconductor industry
body:
The semiconductor industry has been fast growing industry ever since it was introduced because it is the component of every other components we use or come across today from smartphones to electric vehicles to artificial intelligence and quantum computing. Over the past three decades, the industry The industry has just not grown but it has reinvented itself repeatedly. The factors that supported this transformation has been briefed down below.

  The 2000s
  The actual semiconductor revolution began with the transition from vacuum tubes to transistors in the 1948. And with the birth of integrated circuits , followed by microprocessors; this enabled computing ,communication and automation at scale. 

   The industry was broadly divided into: 
i. Analog chips -  Chips processing real world signals
ii. Digital chips - Work on binary, includes the microprocessor, memory and logic devices which powered industries like desktop, telecom, automotive and consumer electronics. 

 Semiconductor fabrication involves 400+ processes. It is broadly divided into front end (wafer fabrication) and back end (testing, packaging.) The key steps involved are wafer manufacturing, oxidation, photo lithography, etching, deposition and ion implantation, metal wiring, EDS process and finally the packaging. The fabrication cost. grew from $10M to $2B+ in 2000s.
   Industry witnessed the deflationary nature as prices dropped with better performance, demand supply mismatch and massive capital investment. The industry relied on technology roadmaps to guided innovation via:
Scaling trends prediction
Problem driven solution

Key challenges in 2000s:
 The lithography was limited to 157 nanometer
Test costs were projected to about $100k/hr
Need for new materials   
Massive funding requirements

 The 2010s: 
The 2010s saw transformation from integrated manufacturing to globally distributed ecosystem. 

The semiconductor production became geographically specialized:
Design: USA, Europe
Fabrication: Taiwan, S.Korea
Assembly and packaging: China. SE Asia
  This led to cost efficiency, faster scaling and global interdependence. 
 
And as the industry divided from all in one to fabless and foundries:
Fabless - companies only focused on the design
Foundries - manufactured the designs provided by fabless
  This led to low entry barriers, faster innovation and emergence of specialized leaders.

    The increased demands in smartphones, tablets and IoTs by consumer demanded energy efficient and high performance chips. At the same time the rise of cloud computing and data centers significantly increased the need for advanced processors, memory semiconductor like DRAM and NAND along with high speed networking hardware laid the foundation for future AI driven systems. Chip design also became increasingly complex, shifting towards multicore heterogeneous architecture thereby requiring sophisticated simulation tools, advanced design software and highly skilled talent. 
   Government began recognizing semiconductors as critical infrastructure and economic drivers. 

 The 2020s

The most recent phase represents shift towards strategy driven dominance. The major reason for the boost being the artificial intelligence; which shifted the demands for data centers, GPUs and accelerators and edge computing devices. Chips are now very essential for machine learning, autonomous systems and advanced computing. 

This market is estimated to be valued at 1.6 trillion by 2030, the economic profit increased by 40 times since early 2000s. The value creation has shifted from traditional manufacturing to architecture, system integration and platform based ecosystems with leading companies investing heavily in R&D, advanced notes and specialized chip designs. This growth however has brought in increased geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, and national efforts to achieve semiconductor self-reliance. As a result the industry is becoming more capital intensive and strategically significant where success depends on technological innovations, bold investment decisions, ecosystem collaboration and global positioning. 

Over the last 30 years the semiconductor industry has evolved from manufacturing technolgy into global innovation and strategic power. The journey of miniaturization guided by Moore’s Law has transformed into complex ecosystem accelerating the force of artificial intelligence. Looking ahead the future of semiconductor industry will be shaped by how effectively it balances innovation, Competition and performance.

title: My Journey into Science
body:
I have always been fascinated by science since I was a child. The journey has been chaotic and, to be honest, I wasn't always as serious as I should have been. Yet, throughout it all, it has been me fighting against myself more than anything else. I have been my greatest companion on this journey, although the outside world has certainly shaped me in many ways. I was curious, emotional, ambitious, confused, and hopeful, often all at once.

If I look back, I think the person who has influenced me the most is Kalpana Chawla. She entered my life at a time when I realized that science was not just a single subject but an entire universe waiting to be explored. There have been many other role models along the way, but she has left the deepest impression on me.

My scientific journey has been anything but linear. It began with my love for organic chemistry, shifted towards physics, wandered into biological sciences, and eventually brought me back to chemistry. Today, I find myself standing at the intersection of multiple disciplines. For the longest time, I kept searching for my "master subject," believing there had to be one field that defined me. But with the rise of interdisciplinary research, and now AI transforming the way we approach science, I have come to realize that perhaps there was never meant to be just one path.
I chose pure sciences after many inspiring conversations with one of my seniors, who shared stories about his research. Listening to his discoveries made me realize that I wanted to become a researcher myself, and somewhere during those conversations, the dream of pursuing a PhD quietly took shape.

Looking back, I don't think I fully realized how much I missed mathematics and physics until I completed my bachelor's degree.. At one point, I even considered preparing for government jobs. However, because of the subjects I had chosen, many opportunities were simply not available to me. It was disappointing, but in hindsight, it nudged me back toward research.
During my bachelor's, I had the opportunity to work on a small research project involving a survey on women with PCOS. Collecting reliable data was far from easy. Social stigma meant that many women were understandably hesitant to disclose accurate information, so we had to work carefully with the responses we received. Despite these challenges, it was an incredibly informative experience. I took the work seriously and eventually submitted a report with conclusions drawn entirely from the survey data. It was my first glimpse into the realities of research, where perfect data is rare and thoughtful interpretation matters just as much.

During my master's, I spent a month at a CSIR laboratory for an internship. That month became one of the most memorable phases of my academic life. I attended a scientific conference, learned to handle NMR instrumentation, and worked on enhancing the curcumin content in oleoresin. I documented the entire work in the form of a detailed report.
More importantly, it was my first real laboratory experience. My guide, the PhD scholars, and the project associates welcomed me warmly, patiently answered my endless questions, and made the entire experience unforgettable. They taught me not only scientific techniques but also what a research environment truly feels like.
After the internship, my work shifted into an interdisciplinary space involving inorganic chemistry, polymers, and applied physics, while allowing me to build upon the analytical chemistry skills I had already developed. Synthesizing the material, confirming its formation, improving its thermal stability, and finally encapsulating the perovskite proved to be challenging at every step. Fabricating it into a triboelectric nanogenerator that could function as a UV sensor made the journey even more exciting.

Synthesizing the material, confirming its formation, improving its thermal stability, and finally encapsulating the perovskite proved to be challenging at every step. Fabricating it into a triboelectric nanogenerator that could function as a UV sensor made the journey even more exciting.

Seeing that work eventually lead to a publication in a Q1 journal felt surreal. It was one of those moments that quietly reminded me why I had chosen research in the first place. Equally memorable was presenting the work at various conferences and symposiums. Every presentation brought a different audience, different questions, and different perspectives. It was stressful, certainly, but it was also incredibly rewarding. Those events taught me how to communicate science, defend my work, network with researchers, and appreciate how collaborative scientific research truly is.

My growing interest in semiconductors eventually led me to apply for a project position at IIT Palakkad. After clearing the interview, I moved there to work on semiconductor-related research. It became another defining chapter of my journey.
For the first time, I was largely on my own as a researcher, with constant guidance from my supervisor and support from wonderful colleagues. Although I had moved to an unfamiliar place, it quickly began to feel like home.

Being at such a prestigious institute also gave me opportunities that I had never imagined. I attended inspiring talks by Prof. H. C. Verma, Arunachalam Muruganantham, and several distinguished scientists from national laboratories and research institutions across India and abroad. Listening to them speak, interacting with researchers from diverse backgrounds, and witnessing their passion for science broadened my perspective far beyond the laboratory. Those experiences strengthened not only my technical understanding but also my confidence, curiosity, and appreciation for the scientific community.

When I look back today, I don't see a perfectly planned journey. I see detours, uncertainty, failures, changing interests, and countless moments of self-doubt. But I also see growth. Every subject I explored, every laboratory I entered, every experiment that failed, every conference presentation that made me nervous, and every conversation with mentors and fellow researchers shaped the scientist I am still becoming.

I don't know exactly where this journey will lead next, and perhaps that's the most exciting part. Science has never been about reaching a final destination. It is about continuing to ask questions, embracing uncertainty, and finding joy in discovering something new every single day.

This is only the beginning.

title: Polymer Surfaces, Adhesion and Interfaces
excerpt: This was the talk that felt closest to the kind of materials and interface questions I already find myself thinking about.
body:
This was probably the talk that connected most directly with the kind of materials questions I already find myself interested in. It focused on polymer surfaces, adhesion, surface modification and interfaces.

One of the first points was that polymers generally have low surface energy, which makes adhesion difficult. Plasma treatment can be used to modify the surface, and plasma itself is an ionised gas. Silanes were also discussed as important adhesion promoters.

I found the distinction between an interface and an interphase useful. An interface is treated as a 2D boundary between two materials with no thickness, while an interphase has a thickness and forms because of interactions between the coating and the substrate.

Another point that stood out was the locus of failure. When we talk about adhesion, it is not enough to know that something failed. We also need to know where it failed, whether at the interface, inside the coating, or somewhere else.

The talk covered surface and interface characterisation methods as well. XPS can be used to study surface chemistry through photoelectrons, while contact-angle measurements give information about the surface.

Inelastic electron tunnelling spectroscopy was also mentioned, including measurements around 4 K for studying molecular and surface behaviour such as interactions involving water.

Superhydrophobicity was another interesting part. A contact angle above 150° is considered superhydrophobic, but a high contact angle alone is not enough. Low tilt angle and low contact-angle hysteresis are also important.

The discussion also moved into acid-base interactions in adhesion. One surface can be acidic and the other basic, and their interaction can contribute to adhesion. SiO₂ was discussed as an acidic surface.

The speaker also covered laser surface treatment and different ways of modifying polymer surfaces.

Dry surface modification included plasma, RF treatment, corona, flame treatment, ozone, UV, X-ray, electron treatment, laser treatment, ion bombardment, casting against another material and even rubbing one material against another. The example of using Teflon to obtain a non-sticky surface showed how much surface treatment can change surface behaviour.

Wet surface modification was also discussed. One question that stayed with me was how long the treatment actually lasts and how stable a modified surface remains. Silanes and other adhesion promoters can be used here as well.

Finally, polymer modification can be used to introduce or expose suitable chemical groups on the surface so that they can interact or react with the material that needs to adhere to it. Surface roughness also plays an important role.

My main takeaway from this talk was that adhesion is not controlled by just one thing. Surface energy, chemistry, roughness, chemical interactions, treatment, interface or interphase formation and the actual locus of failure all matter.

title: Solid-State Batteries: From Materials to the Cell
excerpt: This talk moved from atoms and ion transport all the way up to cells and modules, which made me think about batteries as a materials problem as much as a device problem.
body:
This talk looked at batteries at different levels, from the material and atomic scale to particles, electrodes, cells and finally modules.

Different systems were discussed, including lithium-ion batteries, lithium-metal batteries and solid-state batteries.

One point about solid-state batteries was that some designs can work without a separate anode requirement, which can help with higher energy density and a more compact battery.

Lithium-air batteries were also discussed, along with the reactions involved, and sodium was mentioned as another possible battery system.

A major issue with lithium-metal batteries is protecting the lithium-metal anode. The formation of an insulating or passivating layer such as Li₂O₃ on the electrode surface was discussed.

Other approaches are being explored to lower charging voltage and improve cycle life, including the use of redox mediators.

The speaker compared solid-state systems with liquid-electrolyte systems. Instead of a liquid electrolyte between the electrodes, a solid-state cell uses a solid electrolyte.

One of the major problems is dendrite penetration. Lithium dendrites can grow through the solid electrolyte and eventually lead to failure.

Different cathode materials were also discussed, including Li-Mn and Li-Co systems, with the aim of reducing dependence on expensive materials.

The movement of ions in a solid can happen through different mechanisms, including direct hopping, interstitial hopping and vacancy-mediated hopping. Understanding these mechanisms is important for understanding ionic conduction.

The modelling part was also interesting to me. Parameters such as ionic conductivity, stability, Gibbs energy and other thermodynamic factors can be studied through modelling. COMSOL was mentioned as one of the tools used for simulation.

For sulphide-based solid electrolytes, preparation has to be done carefully, generally inside a glove box, because these materials can degrade quickly when exposed to the environment.

What I liked about this talk was the way it connected the material level to the cell and module level. It showed how ion transport, stability and electrode-electrolyte interactions eventually become device-level problems.

title: Research, Startups and Industry
excerpt: This one was less about a particular material and more about what can happen to research when it moves beyond the academic lab.
body:
This talk was more about what happens around research: technical skills, startups, patents, industry and the connection between academia and real problems.

One idea that stood out was the journey from a patent to a startup. Research does not always have to end as a paper. Sometimes a technology can be taken forward and eventually become a startup. MoleBio was mentioned as an example of a technology-led startup.

The speaker also talked about the importance of building technical skills. Research and startups do not always follow the kind of structured path we usually associate with conventional careers, so having interdisciplinary knowledge can become useful.

AI was also discussed as a tool for saving time. Instead of doing every small task manually, AI can be used to improve productivity. Prompt engineering came up as an important skill because the way we frame a prompt can affect the kind of answer we get.

Another point I found useful was doing internships during a PhD. This can give exposure to industry while continuing research.

A PhD with industrial collaboration was another possibility discussed, where the research itself is connected to an industrial problem.

Overall, this talk made me think about research as something that can move in different directions. Technical skills still matter, but understanding how research connects with patents, startups, industry, AI and interdisciplinary work also matters.

title: Aerospace: Materials, Technology and Careers
excerpt: This was much farther from my immediate research area, but I still found parts of it interesting because of the overlap with materials, AI and how research connects to industry.
body:
This talk was mainly about the aerospace industry, the technologies that are coming up and the different career opportunities in this field.

One of the topics discussed was SAF, sustainable aviation fuel. There was also discussion about Concorde and newer developments in supersonic aircraft, including Boom and its avionics.

High-temperature materials for aircraft engines were another important area. The speaker also talked about smart materials and smart structures and how these can be used in aerospace.

AI and ML are becoming important here as well. Aircraft generate a lot of data during operation, and this in-service aircraft data can be studied using AI and ML. Both structural and non-structural parts can be studied this way.

The idea of a virtual prototype was also discussed, which can help in developing a digital twin of an aircraft or a component. There was a comparison between metallic and composite aircraft, along with technologies such as GD&T and CAD/CAM.

There are also companies working on autonomous aircraft and aerospace technologies. One career point that stood out was that we should not always think only about joining an OEM directly. Networking matters.

For job applications, simply sending an open application may not always be enough. Getting connected with people inside the company and asking for an employee referral can also be useful.

The speaker also discussed opportunities after a career in industry, including research opportunities.

One point I definitely agreed with was the importance of fundamentals. We should build strong fundamentals while also widening the breadth of what we know.

The CV should also be shaped according to the field we want to enter. Constantly changing our subject or research direction can make the profile unclear, so building a clearer profile matters.

Scientific writing was another point that stayed with me. Papers are written for scientists, but scientific information should also be communicated in a way that can reach people outside science.

Other career possibilities such as lab management and opportunities related to NITI Aayog were also discussed.

The talk was outside my immediate area, but it still gave me a broader view of how materials, data, technology and careers can come together in another industry.
